Concept/X_Reasons_Why.description:
This format presents a specific number of compelling reasons why someone should choose the product. Each reason should communicate a meaningful benefit, differentiator, proof point, or aspect of the customer experience. The reasons should work together to build a complete value proposition rather than feeling like an unrelated feature list.

The concept should remain positive and confidence-building. It should not criticize competing products or suggest that customers are making a mistake by considering other options. Visually, the number should become the main hook, followed by bold, quickly understandable reasons supported by icons, demonstrations, product shots, or customer proof. The sequence should create curiosity and encourage viewers to stay until the final reason.

Concept/IG_Stories.description:
This format recreates an Instagram Story that appears to have been posted naturally by a real customer. It should feel like someone casually sharing a product they recently tried rather than a brand presenting a polished advertisement.

The story can feature the product in an everyday environment, such as a bedside table, kitchen counter, work desk, handbag, or morning routine. The copy should focus on why the person tried it, their initial doubts, how it fit into their routine, what they personally noticed, and how the experience made them feel. Text overlays should be short, conversational, and slightly informal, using familiar Instagram Story elements such as captions, emojis, polls, location tags, or question stickers only when relevant. Any customer experience shown must come from genuine, approved feedback.

Concept/Us_Vs_Them.description:
This format compares the product’s overall value proposition with a conventional or alternative approach. Them should represent a broader category, habit, or traditional process, not a named competitor or brand.

The comparison can focus on time, effort, convenience, complexity, total cost, routine compatibility, support, or overall value delivered. It should demonstrate why the product offers a smarter or simpler experience without attacking or undermining alternatives. The tone should be confident, premium, and informative. Visually, the creative should use an instantly understandable side-by-side structure with parallel comparison points. The product should emerge as the stronger choice because of its complete value proposition, not because the competing side has been deliberately misrepresented.

Concept/Venn_Diagram.description:
This format uses a Venn diagram to show how the product brings together multiple qualities that customers usually struggle to find in one solution. Each circle represents a customer need, desirable benefit, or product quality, while the product occupies the overlapping centre.

For example, the circles might represent simplicity, convenience, and structured support. The centre then positions the product as the solution that combines all three. The concept works best when the labels are extremely short and the connection can be understood immediately. The tone should feel clever, visually satisfying, and easy to remember. Avoid overcrowding the diagram with explanations. Supporting copy can clarify why the overlap matters to the customer.

Concept/Dont_Buy_This.description:
This format uses reverse psychology by opening with a bold statement such as Don’t buy this if. The objective is to interrupt scrolling and create immediate curiosity. The statement is then completed with conditions that reveal who the product is and is not intended for.

The exclusions should communicate the product’s positioning rather than insult or shame viewers. For example, the copy might say not to choose the product if someone is unwilling to follow the required routine or expects results without using it correctly. It can also be used to communicate genuine suitability restrictions. The tone should be confident, slightly provocative, and honest. The product reveal should explain why the right customer may find it valuable, turning the negative opening into positive qualification.

Concept/iPhone_Notes.description:
This format presents the advertisement as a personal note written inside the iPhone Notes app. It works especially well for confessions, discoveries, personal checklists, honest observations, or things someone wishes they had known earlier.

The writing should appear natural and personal, as though someone typed it for themselves before deciding to share it. It should not read like polished brand copy placed inside a Notes template. Short paragraphs, unfinished thoughts, checkmarks, simple headings, and selective highlighting can increase authenticity. The note should gradually move from a relatable problem or personal realization to the role the product played. Visually, the familiar Notes interface becomes the creative hook, while the copy carries the story.

Concept/Text_Message.description:
This format communicates the product story through a realistic text-message conversation between two people. The exchange can happen between friends, partners, family members, a customer and coach, or any other relevant relationship.

The conversation should begin with a believable question, observation, or moment of curiosity. The product should enter naturally as part of the response rather than appearing immediately as a forced sales pitch. Messages should be short and written in language people would genuinely use in chat. The exchange can address a common doubt, explain a benefit, or show a recommendation based on personal experience. Visually, the design should closely resemble a familiar messaging interface while keeping names, profile images, timestamps, and personal details anonymised or fictional where required.

Concept/Whiteboard.description:
This format explains a problem, product mechanism, comparison, or step-by-step process using a whiteboard. A person may write, draw, circle, underline, or connect ideas while speaking, making the advertisement feel educational and easy to follow.

The concept should simplify one central idea rather than trying to explain the entire product. Hand-drawn arrows, diagrams, keywords, and simple illustrations can help make the message memorable. The presenter should sound like a knowledgeable guide explaining something clearly, not a salesperson delivering a rehearsed pitch. Visually, movement on the board creates retention, while the final diagram should lead logically to the product or recommended action.

Concept/Low_Stock_Alert.description:
This format uses genuine product availability or inventory urgency to encourage faster action. The creative informs viewers that stock is running low, a batch is close to selling out, or a particular offer has limited availability.

The urgency must be real and verifiable. It should never use fabricated countdowns, false scarcity, or misleading availability claims. The message should quickly explain what is limited, why customers may want to act, and what they should do next. The tone should feel timely and direct without becoming aggressive or desperate. Visual elements can include stock indicators, notification banners, inventory counters, product stacks, or warehouse footage to make the situation easy to understand.

Concept/Were_Sorry.description:
This format opens with a formal or dramatic apology, creating curiosity about what the brand has supposedly done wrong. The apology is then reframed around a positive customer outcome, unexpected demand, or a product benefit.

For example, the brand might apologise for making an existing routine feel unnecessarily complicated once customers discover a simpler approach. The humour should remain grounded and should not trivialise genuine customer problems. The transition from apology to value proposition must be clear, so viewers do not mistake it for a real product issue. Visually, the concept can resemble a corporate statement, public notice, or founder announcement before revealing the positive message.

Concept/Customer_Testimonial.description:
This format uses a real customer’s experience to build trust and show how the product fits into an actual person’s life. The strongest testimonials contain a clear beginning, journey, and outcome rather than functioning as a collection of generic praise.

The story should cover the customer’s original problem, what they had tried before, why they considered the product, how they used it, what they personally experienced, and how they felt afterward. The opening should use the strongest complete proof point or relatable moment for that specific story. The edit should retain the customer’s natural language and personality. Supporting visuals can include progress footage, routine shots, product usage, subtitles, and approved proof. Claims must remain faithful to what the customer genuinely said and experienced.

Concept/New_Vs_Old.description:
This format compares a previous version, routine, belief, or customer experience with the current one. It can show how the product, packaging, process, or customer’s approach has evolved.

Unlike Us vs Them, this concept does not compare the brand against an outside alternative. It compares the brand or customer against their own earlier state. The contrast could be between an old complicated routine and a new structured one, old packaging and improved packaging, or an old mindset and a more sustainable approach. The tone should communicate improvement and progress rather than embarrassment about the past. Visually, use a clear split screen or chronological structure so the change is immediately understandable.

Concept/Breaking_News.description:
This format presents the product message in the visual language of a breaking-news broadcast. A dramatic headline, news ticker, anchor-style delivery, or live update introduces the central development.

The news should be a relevant brand announcement, customer insight, category observation, product update, or surprising fact, not fabricated journalism. The format works because viewers instantly recognise the urgency and importance associated with news coverage. The delivery can be serious or lightly humorous depending on the message. Visually, use recognisable news elements without copying the identity of a real media organisation. The story should quickly move from the headline to why the update matters to the viewer.

Concept/Transformation.description:
This format shows a meaningful change that occurred during the customer’s journey. The transformation can be physical, behavioural, emotional, routine-related, or connected to how the customer feels about their progress.

A strong transformation ad should explain the context behind the change rather than relying only on a before-and-after image. It should include the customer’s initial challenge, what they changed, the role of the product, the effort or routine involved, and the result they personally observed. The tone should be encouraging and realistic, avoiding the suggestion that every customer will experience an identical outcome. Any before-and-after visuals must be genuine, approved, accurately labelled, and presented under comparable conditions.

Concept/Reddit_Style.description:
This format recreates the appearance and writing style of a Reddit post or discussion thread. It works well for detailed personal stories, honest product discoveries, questions, confessions, and community-style recommendations.

The headline should sound like something a real person would post, such as asking for advice, explaining what finally helped, or sharing an unexpected experience. The body copy should be specific, conversational, and slightly unpolished. Comments can be used to raise common questions or add social proof, but they should never be presented as genuine if they were created for the advertisement. The overall creative should feel community-led and information-rich rather than designed like a traditional promotional graphic.

Concept/Case_Of_Emergency.description:
This format presents the product as something to reach for during a familiar, high-friction moment. It often borrows the visual language of Break glass in case of emergency boxes, emergency kits, or urgent-response instructions.

The emergency should be relatable and light enough to avoid creating unnecessary fear. It might refer to a predictable moment when routines commonly break, such as sudden cravings, a packed schedule, or difficulty staying consistent. The product is then positioned as a prepared, structured form of support, not an instant medical rescue. The tone can be playful and dramatic, while the supporting copy explains the actual product role clearly. Visually, the product should remain the unmistakable hero.

Concept/Google_Search.description:
This format begins with a realistic search query that represents something the target customer is actively trying to understand or solve. The query becomes the hook because it mirrors the viewer’s own thoughts.

The search results can then introduce common explanations, helpful information, or the product as a relevant option. The wording should resemble how real people search, including direct questions, doubts, and everyday language. The concept should not falsely imply that Google officially recommends or ranks the product. Visually, the familiar search interface should make the creative instantly relatable, while the narrative moves from question to useful answer and then to the product’s value proposition.

Concept/Problem_Vs_Solution.description:
This format places a clearly defined customer problem alongside the way the product helps address it. The connection between the two sides should be direct, specific, and understandable within seconds.

The problem side should show a recognisable moment, frustration, or repeated behaviour rather than using broad statements. The solution side should explain the relevant role of the product without exaggerating its capabilities. Multiple problem-solution pairs can be included, but each pair should remain concise. Visually, the concept may use split screens, arrows, paired cards, or a before this and try this structure. The tone should be empathetic and practical, helping viewers feel understood rather than blamed.

Concept/Side_Effect.description:
This format uses the phrase side effect as a curiosity-driven hook before revealing an unexpected positive change or secondary benefit customers may notice from following the product routine.

Because the term can carry medical implications, the creative must clearly distinguish between an actual medical side effect and a playful communication device. It must not claim guaranteed outcomes or imply that an unverified benefit is medically established. A safer execution may use wording such as an unexpected change customers talk about or what else they noticed. The concept should be based on genuine product truth or approved customer feedback. The tone can be surprising and playful, but the explanation should remain responsible and accurate.

Concept/Bundle_Offer.description:
This format demonstrates the complete value customers receive when purchasing a bundle. Instead of showing only the discounted price, it should explain what is included, how the components work together, and why the bundle offers a more complete experience.

Each item should be visually identified, accompanied by a short explanation of its role. Any additional support, guide, tracker, service, or bonus should be shown separately so the total value is easy to understand. The creative can compare the individual value with the bundle value when accurate. The tone should feel generous, transparent, and value-led. The offer conditions, validity, exclusions, and final price should be clearly communicated without relying on misleading anchoring.

Concept/Stat_Headline.description:
This format uses one powerful statistic as the main headline. The number should immediately communicate the scale of a customer problem, market behaviour, product result, or relevant insight.

The statistic must come from a reliable, clearly identifiable source or approved internal data. The supporting copy should explain what the number means and why it matters to the viewer rather than leaving it without context. If the data comes from a brand survey or customer sample, that should be stated. Visually, the statistic should dominate the creative, with minimal surrounding information. The product then appears as the relevant response, option, or next step, not as proof of a connection the data does not actually establish.

Concept/Doodle.description:
This format uses hand-drawn illustrations, arrows, circles, annotations, and playful visual marks to explain the customer problem or product experience. The doodles add movement and personality while directing attention toward important parts of the creative.

The concept can be used over product photography, lifestyle footage, screenshots, or a plain background. Each doodle should have a communication purpose, such as highlighting a benefit, pointing to a product component, illustrating a thought, or showing a simple process. The overall effect should feel spontaneous and human rather than childish or visually chaotic. Copy should remain short because the drawings already carry part of the explanation.

Concept/Hack_101.description:
This format presents the product or a related behaviour as a practical hack that makes a common challenge simpler. The opening should promise one useful lesson, shortcut, or improvement that the viewer can understand quickly.

The content should first explain the familiar problem, then reveal the hack, demonstrate how it works, and connect it naturally to the product. The product should not be forced into an unrelated tip. The advice must be genuinely useful and should not oversimplify a serious health or lifestyle issue. The tone should be energetic, educational, and easy to apply. Visuals can include step numbers, demonstrations, screen recordings, or a quick do this instead comparison.

Concept/Email_Screenshot.description:
This format presents the advertisement as a screenshot of an email sent by a customer, founder, coach, team member, or relevant stakeholder. It works particularly well for storytelling, personal discoveries, customer questions, and thoughtful recommendations.

The subject line acts as the hook and should create enough curiosity to make viewers read the body. The email itself should sound like genuine correspondence, with a clear reason for being written. It may explain a customer experience, answer a common doubt, share an update, or reveal the thinking behind the product. The format should remain readable on mobile, with unnecessary interface details removed. Any real personal information must be anonymised, and fictional emails should not be misrepresented as genuine customer communication.

Concept/Dont_Be_An_Idiot.description:
This format uses deliberately provocative language to challenge an unhelpful belief, common mistake, or poor decision pattern. Its purpose is to interrupt passive scrolling and make the viewer reconsider what they are currently doing.

The creative should never directly call the customer stupid or humiliate someone for struggling. The criticism should be directed at the mistake, myth, or behaviour, not the individual. After the provocative hook, the copy should quickly explain why the common approach may be ineffective and introduce a more sensible alternative. The tone can be bold and slightly confrontational, but it must remain constructive. If the phrase feels too insulting for the brand, it can be adapted to Don’t make this mistake.

Concept/Meme.description:
This format uses a recognisable meme structure to communicate a relatable customer thought, frustration, or experience. The humour should come from a genuine behavioural insight rather than simply placing product copy on a popular image.

A strong meme ad makes the target customer feel immediately understood. The product can appear as the resolution, reaction, or contrasting situation, but the sales message should remain light. The visual should be easy to process and the text should be short enough to understand without pausing. The tone can be humorous and culturally relevant while still respecting the customer’s struggle. Avoid using copyrighted characters or templates when usage rights are unclear. An original meme-style execution is often safer and more distinctive.

Concept/Trustpilot_Reviews.description:
This format uses genuine Trustpilot reviews to build credibility through independent customer feedback. The review itself should remain the centre of the creative, supported by the product and minimal brand messaging.

Reviews should be reproduced accurately, without altering their meaning or selectively editing them into stronger claims. The reviewer’s personal information should be handled appropriately, and the date, rating, or verification label should only be shown if accurate. Multiple reviews can be grouped around one theme, such as convenience, support, routine, or satisfaction. The tone should feel transparent and proof-led. The visual may borrow Trustpilot’s recognisable review structure, but it must not imply a rating, endorsement, or platform relationship that does not exist.

Concept/Text_On_Skin.description:
This format places handwritten or digitally overlaid text directly on a person’s skin, usually on the hand, arm, shoulder, face, or stomach. The physical placement makes the message feel personal, intimate, and difficult to ignore.

The text should be extremely short, usually a question, feeling, label, or core realization. It may represent an internal thought the person carries, a problem affecting their confidence, or a message they want others to notice. The product story should be explained through the caption, voiceover, or subsequent frames rather than overcrowding the body with copy. The execution must remain respectful and should not shame the person’s body or turn a sensitive concern into a visual spectacle.

Concept/Native.description:
This format is designed to look and feel like the organic content people already consume on the platform. Rather than resembling a polished advertisement, it should match the usual camera style, pacing, captions, framing, and language of native social content.

The content may take the form of a casual talking-head video, routine vlog, unboxing, personal update, demonstration, or response to a comment. The product should enter naturally through the story or daily routine. Minor imperfections, natural lighting, and conversational delivery can increase authenticity, but the message still requires a clear hook and narrative. The objective is to reduce resistance by making the content useful or relatable before it feels promotional.

Concept/Claymation.description:
This format uses clay characters, products, objects, or environments to create a distinctive stop-motion advertisement. It is useful for explaining processes, personifying customer problems, or presenting product components in an imaginative way.

The creative should be built around simple movements and a clear visual idea because complex explanations can become difficult to follow in clay animation. Problems can be represented as characters or objects, while the product helps change the situation. The tone should feel playful, crafted, and memorable, but the product information must remain accurate. Product packaging should be reproduced carefully so essential brand details are not distorted. Short captions or voiceover can provide clarity without competing with the animation.

Concept/AI_Podcast.description:
This format recreates a short podcast-style discussion between hosts, experts, customers, or fictional characters. The conversation is designed to introduce a customer problem, challenge a belief, or explain the product through a natural exchange.

The most compelling statement should appear at the beginning, followed by enough context to make the clip understandable without watching a full episode. The conversation should sound spontaneous and should include disagreement, curiosity, or follow-up questions where appropriate. If the speakers are AI-generated, the creative should not falsely present them as real experts or real customer endorsements. Visually, use microphones, captions, reaction shots, and clean speaker changes to create the feeling of an authentic podcast clip.

Concept/Tier_List.description:
This format ranks behaviours, options, product qualities, routine elements, or customer choices across recognisable tiers such as S, A, B, C, and D. The ranking creates curiosity because viewers want to see where each item will be placed.

The criteria behind the ranking should be clear and consistent. The product should not automatically be placed at the top without explaining why. A presenter can move items into different tiers while offering short, useful reasoning. The tone can be opinionated, entertaining, and educational, but claims must remain fair and accurate. Visually, the familiar tier-board layout should remain uncluttered, with each item large enough to understand on mobile.

Concept/Zero_Stars.description:
This format opens with an apparent zero-star review, creating immediate surprise and tension. The negative-looking opening is then revealed to be humorous, ironic, misunderstood, or based on an expectation the product was never intended to meet.

The reversal must happen quickly so the creative does not accidentally leave viewers with a negative impression. For example, the complaint might jokingly describe an inconvenience created by a positive experience. This concept should never fabricate a real review or disguise brand-written copy as independent feedback. The tone should be witty and self-aware. The final message must clearly communicate the actual value proposition and leave the viewer with a positive understanding of the product.

Concept/Greenscreen.description:
This format features a presenter speaking in front of screenshots, videos, articles, reviews, comments, product pages, or visual examples. The background supplies evidence or context while the presenter explains what viewers should notice.

The presenter should actively point to, react to, or break down information on screen rather than simply standing in front of a static image. The concept works well for answering questions, responding to comments, analysing common mistakes, or explaining product details. The opening should identify one clear topic, and each background change should support the narration. Any external material shown must be accurate, appropriately sourced, and used with the necessary permission.

Concept/X_Signs.description:
This format presents a specific number of signs that indicate the viewer may be experiencing a particular problem or pattern. Each sign should feel familiar enough for the target customer to recognise themselves.

The opening should clearly state what the signs relate to, while each subsequent point should add a new dimension rather than repeating the same idea. The final section connects the pattern to the product’s relevant role or offers the next appropriate action. The concept must avoid diagnosing a medical condition based on general symptoms. The tone should be helpful and validating rather than alarming. Visually, use numbered scenes, checkmarks, short demonstrations, or familiar everyday situations to make each sign easy to recognise.

Concept/Myth_Vs_Fact.description:
This format challenges a common misunderstanding by placing a widely held belief against a clearer, evidence-based explanation. The myth becomes the hook, while the fact provides education and reframes how viewers think about the problem.

Each creative should usually focus on one major myth or a small number of closely related myths. The fact should not become an equally broad or unsupported claim. It should be grounded in approved product information, credible evidence, or appropriately qualified expert guidance. The product can then be introduced as an option aligned with the corrected understanding. Visually, use an unmistakable myth and fact contrast with different colours, crossed-out statements, or a reveal transition.

Concept/Crossed_Out_Problems.description:
This format presents a visible list of customer frustrations and crosses them out one by one as the product’s relevant benefits are introduced. The progressive removal creates a satisfying visual sense of relief and resolution.

The listed problems should be specific, recognisable, and genuinely connected to the product. Crossing something out should not imply that the issue will always disappear completely unless that outcome is supported. Safer wording can focus on reducing friction or making a routine easier to follow. The copy should remain minimal, allowing the crossing-out action to carry the concept. The tone should feel optimistic and empowering, with the final frame showing the product and the simpler state it is designed to support.

Concept/You_Can_Avoid.description:
This format identifies an unwanted situation, mistake, expense, frustration, or routine breakdown that the viewer may be able to avoid by making a better-informed choice.

The creative should begin with the negative situation and explain why it commonly occurs. It should then show the preventive action or more suitable alternative, followed by the product’s relevant role. The message should help customers feel prepared rather than frightened. Avoid exaggerated warnings or suggesting that the product guarantees protection from complex medical or life outcomes. Visually, a before-it-happens scenario, checklist, timeline, or two-path structure can make the prevention logic easy to understand.

Concept/Us_Vs_Us.description:
This format compares the brand or product with its own previous version, alternative plan, package, or offering. It demonstrates progress without relying on an external competitor.

The comparison could show how the product has become simpler, more complete, better supported, easier to use, or more suitable for a particular need. It can also compare two genuine offerings from the same brand to help customers understand which one is appropriate for them. Both sides should be represented honestly. The purpose is to communicate evolution or choice, not make one existing product look intentionally poor. Visually, use parallel columns with identical criteria so the improvement or distinction is immediately clear.

Concept/Warning.description:
This format begins with a strong cautionary message that alerts viewers to a common mistake, misleading belief, unsuitable expectation, or important product consideration. The warning creates urgency by signalling that the following information matters.

The creative should explain what the viewer needs to be careful about, why it matters, and what they can do instead. It can also communicate genuine eligibility restrictions, correct usage requirements, or situations where the product should not be chosen. The tone should be serious and direct without relying on fear, shame, or exaggerated consequences. Visually, warning symbols, high-contrast text, alert notifications, or caution-tape elements can establish urgency, while the supporting message provides calm and responsible guidance.
